hops.afterHeading: The engine: from a bent bundle to a pushing cell
hops.title: A prestin family tree puts dolphins next to bats
hops.text: On a family tree built from prestin's protein sequence alone, researchers found something funny: the bottlenose dolphin left its real relatives and settled in among echolocating bats. Bats and toothed whales evolved biosonar separately, one hunting in night air and the other in the sea, and both listen for very high-pitched echoes. Prestin is the outer hair cell motor that helps mammals hear faint high-frequency sounds. In 2010, two groups reported that dolphin and echolocating-bat prestin sequences group together, and one found evidence that natural selection drove the matching amino-acid changes. So on this one gene, the tree files a dolphin under bats.

sources.citation: Li, Y., Liu, Z., Shi, P., & Zhang, J. (2010). The hearing gene Prestin unites echolocating bats and whales. Current Biology, 20(2), R55-R56.
Liu, Y., Cotton, J. A., Shen, B., Han, X., Rossiter, S. J., & Zhang, S. (2010). Convergent sequence evolution between echolocating bats and dolphins. Current Biology, 20(2), R53-R54.

hops.afterHeading: What the structures can and cannot show
hops.title: Aspirin once quieted the sounds volunteers' ears made
hops.text: The salicylate in that human prestin structure has a homely connection: your body turns aspirin into salicylate. Its effect on the ear showed up in people long before anyone pictured the protein. In 1984, Dennis McFadden and H. S. Plattsmier studied volunteers whose ears gave off faint, steady tones of their own, picked up by a microphone in the ear canal. While the volunteers took aspirin, the tones faded and vanished in every one: small ones within 14 to 20 hours, larger ones within 40 to 70. After the aspirin stopped, the tones came back, in some ears within a day and in others over several days.

sources.citation: McFadden, D., & Plattsmier, H. S. (1984). Aspirin abolishes spontaneous oto-acoustic emissions. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 76(2), 443-448.
Ge, J., Elferich, J., Dehghani-Ghahnaviyeh, S., et al. (2021). Molecular mechanism of prestin electromotive signal amplification. Cell, 184(18), 4669-4679.
DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine). Aspirin and omeprazole delayed-release tablets, prescribing information, section 12.3: aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is hydrolyzed to salicylic acid.

hops.title: Listen for a third note nobody is whistling
hops.text: Find a friend and a quiet room. Each of you whistles a steady high note, close in pitch, at a comfortable volume, never loud enough to hurt or leave your ears ringing. Then whoever has the higher note slides it slowly upward. Some people hear a faint extra tone sliding downward that nobody is whistling; if you don't, that is common, so don't push the volume. Giuseppe Tartini, an Italian violinist, described this phantom note in a 1754 treatise and later wrote that he had first heard it in 1714. Part of it can come from your own cochlea, whose nonlinearity makes combination tones such as 2f1 - f2.

sources.citation: Alonso, R. G., Gianoli, F., Fabella, B., & Hudspeth, A. J. (2025). Amplification through local critical behavior in the mammalian cochlea. PNAS, 122(29), e2503389122.
Jaramillo, F., Markin, V. S., & Hudspeth, A. J. (1993). Auditory illusions and the single hair cell. Nature, 364(6437), 527-529.
Tartini, G. (1767). De' principj dell'armonia musicale contenuta nel diatonico genere. Padua (chapter 1, §3: discovery in Ancona in 1714).

image.caption: Two steady whistles can let your nonlinear cochlea make a faint third note of its own.
